claims.text: Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi typically produces significant residual thermal stresses in miniature components.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing compromises the microstructure of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Replacing high-thermal-load additive manufacturing with debinding followed by controlled solid-state sintering can overcome residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi components.
Debinding followed by controlled solid-state sintering can overcome degraded mechanical properties in AlCrFeNiSi components.
Debinding eliminates volatile compounds from the shaped AlCrFeNiSi powder body.
Comparing ambient-air and vacuum debinding can reduce non-uniform surface oxidation.
Low-temperature solid-state sintering promotes particle-neck formation in AlCrFeNiSi powder compacts.
Low-temperature solid-state sintering promotes densification of AlCrFeNiSi powder compacts.
A sintering temperature below 1200 degrees Celsius is sufficiently below the melting point to avoid full melting while permitting adequate solid-state diffusion.
The proposed route is applicable to AlCrFeNiSi components with a characteristic dimension below 1 cm.
Controlled debinding reduces stress-inducing gaseous by-products.
Controlled debinding removes deleterious and inconsistent surface oxide layers.
Solid-state sintering produces gradual densification and stress relaxation.
Reduced residual stress and optimized grain-boundary diffusion produce more uniform microstructural evolution and improved particle bonding.
The debinding-plus-sintering route will yield lower residual thermal stresses than conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
The debinding-plus-sintering route will yield higher tensile strength than conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
The debinding-plus-sintering route will yield higher ductility than conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Temperatures above 1200 degrees Celsius or overly rapid heat treatments may prevent the intervention from producing the intended diffusion-mediated benefits.
